scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

A suit can encourage better posture (shoulders back, chin up), which often correlates with confidence. Even if you’re not aware of it, your body language might be more assertive when dressed this way. 3. **Psychological Priming**: Studies (like those on "enclothed cognition") suggest that certain clothes can subtly affect your mindset. Wearing a suit might make you feel more "in control" or "serious," which can boost your confidence in high-stakes situations. 4. **Social Perception**: People often judge competence based on appearance. If you feel confident *and* others perceive you as authoritative, it can create a positive feedback loop—reinforcing your self-assurance. 5. **Personal Identity**: Confidence isn’t just about outward appearance; it’s also about aligning with how you want to be seen. If a suit feels like "you," it’s a tool for self-expression, not just a uniform. **Potential Considerations**: - **Context Matters**: A suit might feel stifling in creative or casual environments. Balance it with outfits that reflect your personality too. - **Comfort**: If it’s too tight or uncomfortable, confidence can dip. Find a fit that’s polished but *yours*. - **Authenticity**: Confidence comes from within, but clothes can amplify it. If you’re not naturally drawn to formalwear, explore other styles that make you feel powerful (e.g., sharp blazers, tailored coats). **Try This**: Next time you wear a suit, notice how it affects your interactions. Do you speak more clearly? Do others respond differently? Experiment with small tweaks (e.g., a bold tie, a pocket square) to see what enhances your vibe. Ultimately, if it works for you, lean into it! Confidence is a skill—dressing in a way that supports it is just one part of the equation. What’s your favorite part about wearing a suit? The fit? The ritual of dressing up?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This scenario touches on **gender roles, responsibility, communication, and personal boundaries**—all of which are valid concerns. Here’s my breakdown of whether you’re **AITA (Against It)** or not, along with the reasoning: ### **Score: 1 (But with nuance)** *(Not fully "wrong," but there’s room for improvement in how you handle it.)* --- ### **Why Not Fully "Wrong"?** 1. **You’re Not Obligated to Be Her Personal Mechanic** - You’ve already gone above and beyond by teaching her how to check tire pressure and showing her the basics. Continuing to do her car work for her—especially when she’s refusing to learn—isn’t fair to you. **You’re not her servant**, and she shouldn’t expect you to be her default "fixer." 2. **You’re Teaching Her (Even If She Doesn’t Want to Learn)** - You’ve already taken steps to empower her (buying a PSI gauge, showing her how to pump air). If she refuses to engage, that’s on her, not you. **You can’t force someone to learn**, but you’ve done your part. 3. **You’re Setting Boundaries (Which Is Healthy)** - You’ve made it clear that you won’t be her go-to for car repairs, and you’re not backing down. **Standing firm on your limits is important**—especially in a relationship where one person is expected to handle everything. 4. **You’re Not Judging Her for Being a Woman—You’re Judging Her for Being Irresponsible** - Your frustration isn’t about gender; it’s about **her refusal to take basic responsibility for her own car**. That’s a fair point. --- ### **Why It’s Still Problematic (And How to Improve)** 1. **You’re Not Just Refusing—You’re Withholding Help Entirely** - While you’re right to set boundaries, **completely refusing to help** (even if she’s being unreasonable) might come across as punitive. Instead of saying *"I won’t do it,"* try: - *"I won’t keep doing this for you, but if you’re stranded, you’ll need to know how to handle it yourself."* - *"I’m not your mechanic, but if you want to learn, I’ll show you again—but you have to actually try this time."* 2. **You’re Missing a Chance to Guide Her (Without Nagging)** - Instead of just refusing, you could **frame it as a safety lesson**: - *"If you don’t learn this, you might get stranded. Do you want me to show you one more time, or are you okay with relying on strangers?"* - This keeps you from being the "bad guy" while still making her accountable. 3. **Her "Real Men" Argument Is a Red Herring** - The fact that her male friends/family agree with her doesn’t make it right. **Real men don’t enable dependency—they encourage self-sufficiency.** If she’s comfortable with outdated gender roles, that’s her choice, but **you shouldn’t have to play along just to avoid conflict.** 4. **You Could Offer a Compromise (Without Doing the Work for Her)** - Instead of a full refusal, you could say: - *"I won’t pump your tire every time, but if you’re really struggling, I’ll help you find a mechanic who can fix the leak properly."* - This keeps you from being the "rescuer" while still ensuring the problem gets solved. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (But With a Caveat)** - **You’re not wrong for refusing to be her default mechanic**, but **how you handle it matters**. - **A better approach** would be to **set boundaries firmly but offer guidance** (without doing the work for her). - **Her refusal to learn is on her**, but **your refusal to help entirely might come off as harsh**—especially if she’s genuinely struggling. **Would you rather:** - **Keep refusing entirely** (and risk her resentment or feeling abandoned)? - **Offer one last chance to learn** (but make it clear she has to actually try)? - **Find a middle ground** (e.g., helping her find a mechanic but not pumping the tire)? **What’s the bigger issue here?** Is this about **control, fairness, or just not wanting to be her "fixer"?** That might help shape the best response.
